title: Cu2O/CuO Electrocatalyst for Electrochemical Reduction of Carbon Dioxide to Methanol
abstract: Herein, we report the controlled and direct fabrication of Cu2O/CuO thin film on the conductive nickel foam using electrodeposition route for the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) to methanol. The electrocatalytic reduction was performed in CO2 saturated aqueous solution consisting of KHCO3, pyridine and HCl at room temperature. CO2 reduction was carried out at a constant potential of −1.3 V for 120 min to study the electrochemical performance of the prepared electrocatalysts. Cu2O/CuO shows better electrocatalytic activity with highest current density of 46 mA/cm. The prepared catalyst can be an efficient and selective electrode for the production of methanol.

sections.text:
Herein, we report the controlled and direct fabrication of Cu2O/CuO thin film on the conductive nickel foam using electrodeposition route for the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) to methanol. The electrocatalytic reduction was performed in CO2 saturated aqueous solution consisting of KHCO3, pyridine and HCl at room temperature. CO2 reduction was carried out at a constant potential of −1.3 V for 120 min to study the electrochemical performance of the prepared electrocatalysts. Cu2O/CuO shows better electrocatalytic activity with highest current density of 46 mA/cm2. The prepared catalyst can be an efficient and selective electrode for the production of methanol.
Keywords: Electrodeposition; Cu2O/CuO; Electrochemical CO2 reduction; CH3OH

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
In the past few years, the pollution level in the atmosphere has increased severely because of the uncontrollable rise in the CO2 emission. The main reason for this undemanding increase in CO2 emission is the burning of the fossil fuels [1]. In this regard, much effort has been put on many levels so far to lower the CO2 content from the atmosphere. Considering the various efforts/measures in this regard to lessen CO2 discharge at the first place is to convert it back to fuel or any other useful chemicals [2,3]. There is already a known technique called Carbon Capture and Utilization (CCU) which is being utilized for capturing CO2 and further convert it into some other useful chemicals. With this approach, the CO2 level in the atmosphere will not only be decreased but also that will solve the current and future energy crisis issues [4].
To convert CO2 into value-added chemicals,
various techniques have been proposed so far namely, thermochemical [5], photocatalytic [6], photoelectrochemical [7], and electrochemical reactions [8–16]. Among all these routes, electrochemical method stands out to be the best because it is more economic, compact in size, can be easily controlled by applying electrode potentials and the electricity can be used for the reaction to take place can be the renewable sources of energy like solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, and thermoelectric without producing any new CO2 into the atmosphere [17–19]. To reduce CO2 by using electrochemical route is a potential strategy to transform the recurrent sources of energy into convenient and value-added chemicals [20,21].
Therefore, novel electrocatalysts are needed to
reduce CO2 to other value-added products using electrochemical method which can operate at room temperature [2,22]. In recent studies, a lot of electrocatalysts have been used, including metals, metal oxides, transition metal chalcogenides, and carbon-based materials for the electrochemical reduction of CO2. Particularly, most of the studies have been dedicated to controlled synthesis of electrocatalysts in terms of their size, shape, and morphology. Nevertheless, looking for new and effective electrodes could be still an important strategy to meet the criteria for practical applications [23]. Among the different catalysts experimented as of now, Cu has shown a distinctive ability to run the electroreduction of CO2 to valued products [4,24–29]. Cu outstandingly promotes the production of hydrocarbons at higher rate over long period of time which makes it as the best electrocatalyst for the CO2
reduction [30,31]. Though Cu can be considered as a unique candidate but it generates a range of products where selectivity of each product is small [32]. To overcome these issues, several efforts have been dedicated to improve the selectivity and current density for the successful electrochemical CO2 reduction to a specific product over Cu-based electrocatalysts, Cucomplexes, nanostructured Cu, oxide-derived Cu, and Cu-alloys [23]. The surface of Cu-oxide provides both the intermediate hydrogen overpotentials and CO adsorption properties that allow production of high yields of CH3OH in aqueous solutions [25]. Le et al. electrodeposited cuprous oxide thin film and they were able to reduce CO2 to CH3OH with yields of 43 μmol cm−2 h−1 and Faradaic efficiencies of 38 % in 0.5M KHCO3. They proposed that Cu(I) species are highly responsible for the selective production of CH3OH [26]. In an another study, Malik et al. reported synthesis of Cu2O supported over functionalized MWCNT for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 and they achieved a faradaic efficiency of 38 % at −0.8V for methanol production [33].
The electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CH3OH
involves the requirement of 6 electrons to undergo the reaction which makes the reduction process kinetically unfavorable [15,16]. To overcome this issue, many efforts have been taken in previous studies where nitrogen-containing heterocycles like pyridinium ion has been used to reduce the overpotentials [3,4,34]. In 1994, Bocarsly and co-workers reported the use of pyridinium ion as a novel homogeneous catalyst for the successful reduction of CO2 to CH7OH at a Pd electrode with low overpotential [35]. Recently, Albo et al. used a series of pyridine derivatives as co-catalysts for the electroredution of CO2 to CH3OH at Cu2O/ZnO based-electrodes. They reported a maximum methanol formation when using 2- methylpyridine with Faradaic efficiency of 16.86 % at overpotential of 200 mV [4].
Herein, we report the electrodeposition of
binder-free Cu-based oxide electrodes for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CH3OH. We prepared a series of Cu−based oxide electrocatalysts annealed at different temperatures. The as-prepared Cu2O/CuO catalyst has not been used in the past for the electrochemical reduction of CO2. Cu2O/CuO electrocatalyst showed high current density, significant stability during the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction for longer period of time and the catalyst was selective towards the production of CH3OH.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text: Copper sulfate (CuSO4·5H2O, 98+ %, Acros Organics), sulfuric acid (H2SO4, 95 %, Across Organics), potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3, 99 %, Alfa Aesar), pyridine (C5H5N, 99+ %, Alfa Aesar) and hydrochloric acid (HCl, 37 %, Sigma Aldrich) were obtained from different manufacturers. All chemicals were used for the experiment as received without any further purification.

sections.heading: 2.2. Preparation of catalysts
sections.text:
Firstly, a piece of Ni foam was cleaned in 1 M HCl solution to remove the impurities from the surface. Then, the Ni foam was cleaned in ethanol, and distilled water successively for 10 min in an ultrasonic bath, followed by drying in air at 80 °C in an oven for 12 h. The thickness of the Ni foam is 1 mm and it was purchased from QiJing Trading Co., Ltd Store, China. Electrodeposition of Cu on Ni foam was carried out by using our previously reported method [36]. 0.05 M of CuSO4.5H2O and 0.1 M of H2SO4 were dissolved in 100 ml distilled water. The as-prepared solution was used as the electrolyte for the electrodeposition of copper on conductive Ni foam with an exposed area of 1 × 1 cm. A platinum wire and an Ag/AgCl (1 M KCl) electrodes were used as a counter electrode and reference electrode, respectively. The potentiostatic electrodeposition of Cu on Ni foam was performed at a constant potential of −0.9 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) for 60 s. After the complete deposition for 60 s, the Ni foam was taken out of the electrolyte solution and carefully washed with deionized water and ethanol and then dried at 60 °C.
Subsequently, the electrodeposited Cu/Ni films were annealed in air at different temperatures such as 100, 200,
300 and 400 °C for 2 h, and the samples were named as Cu100, Cu200, Cu300 and Cu400, respectively.

sections.heading: 2.3. Characterizations
sections.text:
The binder free as-prepared electrocatalysts were characterized by different physico-chemical techniques like X-ray diffraction (XRD), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM) equipped with EDS and transmission electron microscope (FE-TEM). The crystallinity of the Cu-oxide films were recognized using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Shimadzu XRD-6000) with Cu K-alpha irradiation (λ = 1.5406 Å) for 2θ values from 20° to 80°. Surface chemical valence states were characterized using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS Thermo, Esca lab 250xi). To get a clear idea of the shape and morphology of the Cu-oxide samples, field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, Sigma S-4000) was performed. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Philips CM 200) and selected area diffraction (SAED) were also executed for high resolution observation.
2.4. Procedure of electrochemical reaction for CO2 reduction The electrochemical CO2 reduction was carried out in a laboratory-made customized H-type cell made up of glass as shown in Figure 1. The conditions used for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 are shown in Table 1. The cathode and the anode compartments were separated by an ion exchange membrane (Nafion Membrane N117). Commercial Ni foam, Ag/AgCl (1 M KCl) electrode and Pt wire were used as the working electrode, reference electrode, and counter electrode, respectively. All the electrochemical experiments for CO2 reduction were performed at room temperature and the electrolyte in both the cathode and the anode compartment was an aqueous solution of 0.5 M KHCO3 and 10 mM of pyridine. To bring down the pH of the solution to 5, required amount of HCl was added dropwise. To perform the experiment in acidic medium, this study was mainly focused on just one intermediate pH value (here 5) to understand the catalytic behavior of all the electrocatalysts. Studies suggest that CO2 can be reduced electrochemically to other hydrocarbons selectively in acidic electrolytes [37– 39]. Subsequently, cyclic voltammetry (CV), chronoamperometry (CA), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests were carried out. Before the electrochemical CO2 reduction, the Pt

Figure S2 shows the survey spectrum of all the four electrocatalysts namely Cu100, Cu200, Cu300 and Cu400; all of them indicate the presence of Cu and O elements. From Figure 3a, the peaks located at 932.3 ± 0.4 eV and 952.1 ± 0.3 eV can be attributed to Cu 2p3/2 and Cu2p1/2 of Cu 2p spectrum, which refer to the formation of Cu+. Binding energies of Cu+ and Cu0 phases are same that is why it is difficult to distinguish metallic phase of Cu from Cu+. This result matches with the XRD analysis shown in Figure 2. Additionally, two discreet peaks can also be pragmatically deconvoluted at 933.5 ± 0.2 eV and 952.8 ± 0.4 eV, which can be credited to Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2 phases of Cu2+, indicating the existence of very low content of CuO in the Cu100 film [40–43]. In addition, presence of weak satellite peak attributed to the existence of CuO. This result contradicts with the above XRD interpretation shown in Figure 2, where there is no peak associated with CuO. It is predicted that the topmost surface of Cu100 may possibly be further oxidized to form CuO.
Figure 3b-c show the deconvulated peaks of Cu
2p spectra, attributes to the formation of both Cu2O and CuO phases in deposited electrocatalysts. The two pairs of peaks between binding energies of 930 eV and 940 eV, and 950 eV and 960 eV, indicate the existence of both Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2 peaks of Cu+ and Cu2+. Whereas, the

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrochemical study for CO2 reduction
sections.text:
Electrochemical analysis of all electrocatalysts were conducted by a potentiostat using cyclic voltammetry (CV), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and chronoamperometry (CA) techniques in a customized H-cell (Figure S5). Firstly, double layer capacitance (CDL) and electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) of all the electrocatalysts were calculated by measuring the CV curves at different scan rates in 0.5 M KHCO3. Figure S6 shows the plot of current density versus different scan rates and Figure S7 depicts the corresponding slope which is equal to CDL of the respective catalysts. Table S1 summarizes the CDL and ECSA of all the electrocatalysts where Cu300 showed
highest surface area as compared to other catalysts. It is believed that larger ECSA value provides abundant active sites for the catalytic reactions. All CV measurements were carried out at a scan rate of 30 mV/s between 0 and −1.4 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) to examine the voltammetric behavior of all the prepared electrodes in an electrolyte consisting of 0.5 M KHCO3, 10 mM of pyridine and HCl. To study the effect of presence of dissolved CO2 in the electrolyte, CV tests were done in an electrolyte without and with saturated CO2 (99.99 %).
Figure 6. CV curves of electrocatalysts without CO2 and with saturated CO2 in a potential window of 0 to −1.4 V vs. Ag/AgCl.
Figure 6 demonstrates the CV curves of Cu100,
Cu200, Cu300, and Cu400 electrodes without and with CO2 saturated electrolyte solution. As seen from the figure 6, Cu300 electrode exhibited higher current density values than the other respective electrocatalysts. Consequently, Cu300 electrode showed better performance than other electrodes. There is no major change in the value of the current density in case of the samples Cu100, Cu200 and Cu400 before and after addition of CO2 in the electrolyte. Cu300 has shown significant increase in the current density when the CV was taken in the CO2 saturated electrolyte. There is almost a two times increase in the value of the current density can be seen in case of the sample Cu300. It is reported that the reason for the increased current density is the reduction of CO2 in the CO2 saturated electrolyte [45]. Sample Cu300 consist of both Cu(I) and Cu(II) phases. As a result, there is a formation of heterostructure of Cu(I) and Cu(II) in Cu300 that shows different synergistic relations between these two phases and thus, it improves the functional characteristics of the prepared material. In case of Cu400, two reduction peaks are observed at ‒0.6 V and ‒1.0 V in the absence of CO2, which can be attributed to the transition of CuO to Cu(I) and Cu(I) to Cu, respectively. When the electrolyte was saturated with CO2, the peak at ‒0.6 V disappeared which might be due to the reduction of CuO to Cu at negative potentials and the only reduction peak at ‒1.0 V is mainly ascribed to the CO2 reduction [47].
Figure 7a also shows the CV of bare Ni foam in
the saturated CO2 electrolyte which clearly explains that bare Ni foam has no role in the electrochemical reduction of CO2. Cu300 recorded the highest current density of 46 mA/cm2. Furthermore, EIS analysis was employed to reveal the kinetics of the prepared electrocatalysts at the electrode surface (Figure 7b). The Nyquist plot was recorded from 100 kHz to 1 Hz which reveals the charge transfer behavior of the electrocatalysts. From the Nyquist plot, it can be seen that the charge transfer resistance of Cu300 electrode is smaller with lesser enclosed area of semicircle than other electrodes. Sample Cu300 consist of both Cu(I) and Cu(II) phases. As a result, there is a formation of heterostructure of Cu(I) and Cu(II) which causes a significant decrease in the radius of the arc in the EIS spectrum of Cu300 compared to the other samples. Consequently, the charge transfer resistance of Cu300 decreases which facilitates the
charge transfer from Cu2O/CuO surface to the electrolyte solution. Even though the bulk solution resistance of electrolyte for the Cu400 electrode looks smaller but having the higher charge transfer resistance obstructs its catalytic performance. Thus, the electrical properties of the prepared materials show that Cu300 can be a favorable candidate for the electrochemical reduction of CO2.
Long-term stability is one of the crucial
measures to understand the electrochemical properties of any electrocatalyst during CO2 electro-reduction. To determine the electrochemical performance for Cu-oxide electrodes towards CO2 reduction, electrolysis was carried out at fixed electrode potential of −1.3 V (vs Ag/AgCl) for 120 min where the resulting reduction current density was recorded as shown in Figure 7c. On the whole, the current density started at high value and decreased gradually with time for all the electrodes. Previous reports have revealed that the decreasing nature of current density during the electrolysis is due to the detachment of some of the particles from the electrode surface [25,44]. In case of electrode Cu300, the current initially started approximately at −33 mA/cm2 and declined slowly to −25 mA/cm2 after 100 min of electrolysis, and then it remains constant until 120 min. Similar behavior can be seen in other electrocatalysts as well where the current tends to decrease initially and then it remains constant for rest of the time. Figure 7d demonstrates the graph of comparison of faradaic efficiency of the all the four electrocatalysts.
After 120 min of run of the chronoamperometry
for CO2 reduction over Cu-oxide electrodes, the electrolyte solution was analyzed by GC and HPLC. Methanol was the predominant product produced as a result of CO2 reduction. Apart from methanol there was nothing in the GC spectrum except the presence of pyridine which was already present in the electrolyte. The Faradaic efficiency of electrode Cu300 for methanol was found to be around 6.46 % at −1.3V (vs Ag/AgCl). Table S2 summarizes the comparison of Faradaic efficiencies of different electrocatalysts for electrochemical reduction of CO2 to methanol. In comparison, Cu100, Cu200 and Cu400 showed lowest Faradaic efficiency as compared to Cu300 electrocatalyst. Here, as shown in GC (Figure S8) and HPLC spectra (Figure S9), no any other liquid product was noticed except methanol and the highest Faradaic efficiency was found to be 6.46 % for methanol. Gaseous products have not been tried to detect in this experiment. Therefore, it is believed that the present

Therefore, the obtained results clearly validate that Cu300 could be an efficient and selective electrode for the electroreduction of CO2 to CH3OH. Consequently, considering these results, it is clear that alone Cu2O or CuO cannot be an active catalyst for methanol production.
The proposed mechanism for the electrochemical
conversion of CO2 to CH3OH can be explained as; when a potential of −1.3 V (vs Ag/AgCl) was applied to the catalyst, initially, Cu2+ was reduced to Cu+ and when the CO2 gas molecules come into contact with the catalyst surface, Cu+ was oxidized to form Cu2+. Then, the reaction involves a fast-equilibrium of the formation of CO2− radical, following the conversion of CO2 to the rate determining step of HCOO− species. Coupling of HCOO− intermediates with electrons and protons produces CO gas molecules. Previous study [47] proposes that the CO gas molecules are further adsorbed and complemented by proton adsorption, which can possibly form a surface formyl (HCO) species. Further coupling of proton and electron with HCO group forms CH3O adsorbate. Later, the surface of the Cu2O/CuO catalyst may further support the addition of proton to the CH3O adsorbate, which ultimately produces CH3OH. There may be some CO molecules which get desorbed from the catalyst surface and not participating in the further reaction, resulting in less amount of formation of CH3OH (Scheme 1).
Scheme 1. Possible reaction mechanism for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CH3OH.
Copper oxide is considered as one of the best
electrocatalysts for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to methanol reported so far but the mechanism of the whole reaction is yet to be understood. Kas et al. have proposed that the catalytic activity of the Cu-based electrocatalysts degrades after some period of time due to the decomposition of copper oxide to copper and there is formation of methanol only during such kind of reactions [50]. It can be seen in post-electrolysis XRD analysis of
samples Cu200 and Cu300 as shown in Figure S10, where there are peaks associated with the Cu and Ni (substrate) and there is one peak present for each of Cu2O and CuO. Hence, the catalyst has not been fully decomposed to Cu after the electrolysis. After 100 min of CA test, the current density remained constant till the end of reaction. It is believed that the reaction can still be allowed to run for longer duration of time, because there are studies which have shown Cu/Cu2O/CuO are the active components for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to various other products also [26,42,51]. FE-SEM image of electrode Cu300 did not change significantly except some cracks after 120 min of chronoamperometry run for CO2 reduction (Figure S11). In EDS spectrum, apart from the presence of copper (Cu) and oxygen (O) elements, potassium (K) can also be seen which might be adsorbed on the surface of the electrode from the electrolyte solution during the electrocatalytic process. Post-electrolysis XPS survey of Cu300 also supports the EDS spectrum, showing the presence of K 2p peak (Figure S12a). Figure S12b shows the presence of both Cu+ and Cu2+ in the Cu 2p spectrum of Cu300 electrocatalyst after CO2 reduction process which supports the XRD analysis after reduction.
In a nutshell, there are still various limitations
associated with electrochemical reduction of CO2. It demands to develop a method for electroreduction of CO2 which not only can selectively reduce CO2 into several value-added products but also suppresses the hydrogen evolution. For the efficient and successful reaction to occur there are various aspects which need to be taken into consideration; (a) the design of the reactor needs to be further developed which allows the reaction to happen under high CO2 pressure without any error; (b) synthesis and fabrication of suitable electrocatalysts having better stability during the course of reaction; and (c) type and pH of electrolytes which have high solubility for CO2 and also permits the separation of products after the electrolysis. Therefore, future studies would be focused on to understand the nature of the as-prepared Cu2O/CuO supported on Ni foam substrate towards electrochemical reduction of CO2 in the presence of pyridine in an acidic medium.

basis of the results obtained, it is concluded that choice of electrocatalyst with high current density and enhanced faradaic efficiency is crucial. Electrocatalyst Cu300 showed high current density and better faradaic efficiency as compared to other electrocatalysts. It is believed that the direct growth of mixed phases of Cu2O/CuO on porous Ni foam enhances charge transfer between the current collector and the electrocatalyst showing better electrical properties may be the key reason behind the improved catalytic activity towards CO2 reduction. Though these are the preliminary results but the selection and preparation of the electrode with more complete knowledge of reaction mechanism will open up a new window in the selective reduction of CO2 to CH3OH. Further study can be done to improve the reduction performance of this particular catalyst in a mechanistic way.
